Export of REPORT.md (scripts/export_pdf.py); no results recomputed. Source paths refer to the repository.

LLM private pricing channels raise the price level, with no detected contemporaneous co-movement: dependence statistics (conditioned mutual information) vs level screens on scripted and LLM sellers

Apart AI Collusion Sprint, Q1.4 (action-only, statistical half of "Beyond Words: Detecting AI-Agent Collusion Through Information Theory and Behavioral Evidence"). Every number below is regenerated by the commands in §6 from results/, except explicitly attributed sibling-project numbers (including §4.4; P2.11b's sibling rows are checked against snapshots of their JSON).

Key findings in one minute (plain-language summary; every number is from the text below)

  • A private chat channel raised prices for every seller model we tested: 9/9 sets, 7 models.
  • It shows up as a higher price level, not prices moving together: the co-movement detector (pCMI) is at chance in the 192-game grid (0.51).
  • Even agreements that were actually executed show no co-movement: pCMI 0.42 [0.33, 0.53] on 48 executed games.
  • Level screens are not collusion-specific: they false-flag 30/30 scripted markets with unequal costs and need a model- and prompt-matched reference.
  • At 1% prevalence no flag's point-estimate precision reaches 0.25, so a flag is an audit trigger, not a verdict.
  • Of the dependence statistics, only lagged dependence (TE, 0.62) is weakly above chance, still (barely) below level (paired Δ +0.12 [+0.01, +0.22]), and it sits in channel games whose agreement was not executed (exploratory).

Main claim (v1 + Phase 2). In our LLM pricing markets, assigning a private channel shows up as a sustained price level (spreading to rivals in the gpt-6-luna sets), with no detected contemporaneous co-movement of prices: the channel raised markup over Nash in 9/9 sets (7 seller models; C − A CI > 0 in each), and max-pair markup had a higher point-estimate run AUROC than pCMI in 9/9 (0.75–0.99 vs 0.34–0.72), with the paired Δ level − pCMI CI > 0 in 8/9 sets (E74, declared, same games; per-set 95% CIs, uncorrected; unresolved only for gpt-5.6-luna, +0.03 [−0.27, +0.33]; smallest resolved Δ +0.22 [+0.03, +0.44], base Qwen3.6), while pCMI's CI includes 0.5 in 8/9. This holds at T=60 (pre-registered E44: pCMI 0.34 [0.18, 0.52]), and restricting to executed agreements does not raise pCMI (0.42 [0.33, 0.53], 48 executed games; the level is inflated by construction on that subset, P2.11). Level and co-movement screens fail in opposite places (unequal private costs: level screens false-flag 30/30 scripted markets, pCMI 4/30), and level screens need model- and prompt-matched references, because the no-channel baseline moves with wording and model and is tacit-high (defined below) for an older model (9/10) or under strong profit framing (19/20, Q2.2's arm). The scope is detected co-movement in these markets: at T=60 no co-move excess is detected (+0.004 [−0.007, +0.015]), where pCMI detects a planted shared ±1 move at q = 0.1 (AUROC 0.79 [0.70, 0.88]), but at T=20 (most sets, all of E70) the same planting gives only 0.62 [0.52, 0.71], so small co-movement is not excluded there; this bounds sensitivity to that planting, not to every collusive strategy (P2.8). The null is not specific to the linear-Gaussian estimator: a rank-based (copula) pCMI and a discrete sign-change CMI are also at chance on E70, E44 and the executed-only set (E73, declared robustness, P2.8). Lagged dependence is not excluded: in the registered 16-cell grid (E70, 192 games) transfer entropy is weakly above chance (0.62 [0.54, 0.70]; declared secondary hypothesis confirmed), though below max-pair markup (0.74 [0.66, 0.81]; paired Δ +0.12 [+0.01, +0.22], E74); in an exploratory follow-up (E72) TE names the channel pair in 30/96 games (chance 1/6), and the signal sits in non-executed channel games (0.73) rather than executed ones (0.49; post hoc, difference untested) (P2.14).

Terms (used throughout). C / A = channel / no-channel arm (matched seeds and prompt otherwise). C − A = difference in mean all-seller markup over the per-round Nash price. Max-pair markup (market_level; "level" / "market level" below) = the highest pair's mean price over Nash, a run-level score; pair_level = pair mean minus the other two sellers' mean. pCMI = max-pair Gaussian conditional MI of current prices given public state and all sellers' lagged prices; TE = max-pair, max-direction transfer entropy (lagged dependence, not signed following). Executed = judge-labelled agreement AND both pair firms ≥ agreed − 1 in ≥ ½ of post-agreement rounds AND second-half pair mean ≥ Nash + 2 (our implemented rule, not Q2.2's; 13–78/149 executed under 27 variants, E71). Tacit-high = a no-channel market whose second-half mean is ≥ Nash + 2 (a price threshold, not verified coordination). Co-move excess = the assigned pair's share of same-direction price moves minus the other five pairs' mean (P2.8); q = per-round probability of a planted shared ±1 move. Sign tests are one-sided.

Abstract

Can a prices-only detector find colluding agents without accusing agents sharing a shock or model? We compare dependence statistics (MI, pCMI = Gaussian conditional MI given public state and lagged prices, transfer entropy TE) with price-level screens in a 4-seller price market. Scripted sellers: pCMI flags every planted shared-signal pair and cuts MI's common-shock false alarms from 100% to 14%; level screens fail where pCMI does not (unequal costs: 30/30 vs 4/30 false flags). LLM sellers (9 sets, 7 models, 10–21 games per arm): a private channel raised markup over Nash in 9/9 sets, but as a level: max-pair markup beat pCMI in 9/9 (AUROC point estimates 0.75–0.99 vs 0.34–0.72; paired difference CI > 0 in 8/9), and pCMI's CI included 0.5 in 8/9 (base Qwen3.6 exception, 0.71 [0.51, 0.88], not replicated in E70). Longer games (pre-registered, T=60: pCMI 0.34 [0.18, 0.52]), executed agreements only (48/149; pCMI 0.42 [0.33, 0.53]) and memory (inconclusive) revealed no co-movement. A 16-cell, seven-factor grid (E70, 192 games, public board on) is consistent: C − A positive in 13/16 cells, level > pCMI in 12/16 (point estimates), pooled pCMI 0.51 [0.43, 0.59]; only lagged TE is weakly above chance, 0.62 [0.54, 0.70]; a declared follow-up found no confirmed model effect. With gpt-6-luna the level spreads to rivals. Absolute screens need model- and prompt-matched references: wording moves no-channel markup −0.19 to +2.56; an older model or profit framing makes it tacit-high. Refusal-removed Qwen did not collude detectably more (3/3 pairs). In a double auction, chat barely raised asks (+0.39 [+0.06, +0.69]; detectors inconclusive). At 1% prevalence no flag's point-estimate precision reaches 0.25.

Relative screens survive a shared model but fail under market-wide spillover; absolute screens need model- and prompt-matched references." "With memory and a profit objective, gpt-6-luna sellers raise prices market-wide without any channel (19/20 no-channel markets ≥ Nash + 2); agreements are then often kept (13/20) but add no detectable price, so channel labels stop being ground truth. Phase 2 takeaways (≤ 8; numbers from the rows above and the sections named). (1) Opposite failure modes. Unequal private costs: level screens 30/30 false, pCMI 4/30 (P2.4). LLM channels: mostly a level; pCMI is not significantly above chance in 8/9 sets and 5/5 wordings (exception: base Qwen3.6, 0.71 [0.51, 0.88], P2.11; template 0.17, below chance), while the level screen also fails in two wordings (markup AUROC 0.31, 0.47; P2.7, P2.9). A deployer needs both kinds of statistic plus cost data. (2) Relative screens miss market-wide elevation. pair_level reverses against an all-firm cartel (AUROC 0.26 / 0.25, P2.4), and LLM channel effects spill over to the rivals (E60: llm_v1 rivals +1.86 of the pair's +2.14 by rounds 11–20; E44 T=60 rounds 51–60 +2.24 of +2.47; deepseek pairs keep more of their lead, +2.37 of +5.03; P2.8). Only an absolute markup sees the whole-market level. (3) Absolute screens need a model- and prompt-matched reference. At α = 0.10, a mismatched-model pool gives pCMI 11/21 = 52% false flags vs 3/21 for a fresh model-matched pool (2/21 at α = 0.05); matched model but other wordings: markup power 1/16 (P2.3). The channel effect (C − A markup) is consistent in our five wordings (pooled +0.69, SE 0.17), while the sibling's pair premium vanishes under a terse paraphrase (Q2.2 E78: +0.24 vs +1.75; a different metric; sibling result, not regenerated here); the no-channel baseline is prompt-dependent in both (ours −0.19 … +2.56, P2.7). (4) Level screens detect "a pair singled out by the prompt", not delivered coordination: an undelivered notepad (0/14 agreements) is named 11/15 vs private 12/15 (P2.10); Q2.2 E77 finds notes-to-self yields 0.65 [0.34, 1.32] of the private premium (sibling result, not regenerated here). Deepseek pairs agree 15/15 but follow 3/15, and abandoned pairs still sit +3.23 above rivals (P2.9d). A public board alone raises deepseek no-channel markup by +0.70 [0.23, 1.23] and makes a frozen level screen flag 5/15 of those markets (P2.9e), so the reference must also match the board. (5) pCMI blind spots: collusion predictable from public price history (deterministic bid rotation) is invisible to it (P2.6). Its scripted calibration mostly holds across N = 2/4/6 and three demand elasticities (6.0% [3.8, 9.3] pooled false flags; 9/10 cells pass, elastic/A fails; P2.5). (6) Prevalence: at 1% no flag reaches a point-estimate precision of 0.25 (upper CIs up to 0.68 where flags occur; P2.1): audit triggers, not verdicts. An independent reimplementation reproduces the per-run statistics and all 20 AUROCs (shift-null flags 4/21 vs 5/21, Monte Carlo; P2.2). (7) Long games do not rescue pCMI (E44, pre-registered, decisive for Q1.4). At T=60, pCMI scores 0.34 [0.18, 0.52] (the declared rule rejects AUROC ≥ 0.65); its point estimate falls with game length (0.52 at T=20; change −0.18 [−0.41, +0.05], not significant), while the market level holds at 0.94. Channel pairs show no co-move excess (+0.004 [−0.007, +0.015]), although pCMI separates a planted shared ±1 move at q = 0.1 in the same games (AUROC 0.79). In this set (gpt-6-luna, T=60) channel pairs show a sustained level and no detectable co-move excess (P2.8). The answer is the same when only executed agreements count (pooled pCMI 0.42 [0.33, 0.53], ten sets) and when sellers get memory (E65, T=40: markup AUROC 0.85, pCMI 0.49; declared executed-only test inconclusive, 0.33 [0.02, 0.66], n = 5 executed) (P2.11).

v1 (overnight) key findings

v1 main claim (overnight, frozen). Conditioned dependence (pCMI: how much two sellers' price movements share after accounting for public demand/cost state and all sellers' previous prices) detects collusion that shows up as coordinated price variation while mostly ignoring shared public shocks and shared policies with independent noise (not policy copies that share a random seed). In two LLM pricing markets a private channel shows up mainly as a price level, which these measures are built to ignore, so a one-line level statistic separates channel from no-channel markets far better (AUROC 0.87–0.98 vs 0.45–0.52; 0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect ranking), though it also ranks legitimate partnerships above controls.

Figure 1. (a) Scripted market, locked test seed, within-run shift null (α=0.05): raw MI flags markets where independent sellers share a public shock (100%) or a policy (30%); pCMI (conditioned on public state and lagged prices) flags 10–14% of them (above α; 4% under the control-surrogate null, §4.1) and still flags 100% of colluding markets (shared-signal collusion, s=0.6, the easiest case; 50/50 per group). Policy copies sharing a random seed remain a confound for both. (b) LLM markets: run AUROC of pCMI is near chance (0.5, dashed), while a price-level statistic separates channel from no-channel markets. v1 abstract (overnight, frozen; Phase 2 is summarised in the Abstract above)

Can a detector that reads only prices and public market state find colluding pricing agents without accusing agents that merely share a public shock or a policy? We test pairwise dependence detectors (|Pearson|, MI, CMI given public state, pCMI = Gaussian CMI given state and all lagged prices, lagged CMI/TE) against a within-run shift null and a no-channel control-surrogate null in a 4-seller repeated price market. Scripted agents (locked test seeds, T=100, 50 runs/group): every contemporaneous detector flags and names a planted shared-signal pair in 100% of runs. Raw MI also flags 100% of markets whose sellers share only a public shock; pCMI flags 14% of common-shock markets under the shift null and 4% [1, 13] of held-out shared-policy-plus-shock markets under the surrogate null. Policy copies sharing a random seed (44–100%) and, for TE, public leader-follower pricing (100%) remain confounds. Dependence detects coordinated variation, not agreement. LLM sellers (gpt-6-luna; our market, 74 games, T=20; sibling market, 125 runs, T=12): in our market (llm_v1) a private channel raises markup over Nash by +1.8 versus matched no-channel markets (C − A [1.2, 2.3]), but mainly as a price level. Level statistics separate channel from control runs (run AUROC 0.87–0.98); pCMI is not distinguishable from chance (0.45–0.52), and neither longer games (T=50, 8 vs 8) nor same-model pairs revealed pCMI signal (both underpowered); whether this reflects mainly the level effect or low power at short T remains unresolved. Level screens are not collusion-specific: they rank legitimate public partnerships above controls (0.75) and respond to an offered-but-undelivered placebo channel in the sibling market. Practical reading (a hypothesis, not tested as a pipeline): a cheap level screen as an always-on first stage, with dependence and text audits as second-stage evidence; the detectability of LLM collusion depends on the market and its framing.

Detailed summary (all headline numbers with their caveats)

We build a 4-seller repeated differentiated-price market with public demand/cost shocks and ask whether pairwise dependence detectors that read prices and public market state only (no messages) can find colluding pairs without accusing sellers that merely share a shock or a policy. Detectors: |Pearson|, mutual information (MI), CMI given public state, Gaussian CMI given state and all lagged prices (pCMI), and lagged CMI (TE), each compared with two baselines: the same game with seller price series circularly shifted out of alignment (shift null) and comparable no-channel markets (control-surrogate null). Scripted agents, locked test seeds (T=100, 50 runs/group): every contemporaneous detector flags and localises a planted shared-signal pair in 100% of runs. Raw MI also flags 100% of markets whose independent sellers share a public shock. pCMI flags 14% of them under the shift null. The surrogate null (which uses those markets as its reference pool, so ≈5% there by construction) flags only 4% [1, 13] of held-out markets with a shared policy plus common shock, and 4% with a public leader-follower pair. Two confounds remain: policy copies that share their random seed (48–100% flagged by each contemporaneous detector in Table 4.1; 44% for differenced |Pearson|, §4.1), and lagged matching, where TE flags legitimate leader-follower pricing in 100% of runs. Dependence detects coordinated variation, not agreement. A constant high price (the tested stay-high setting) was not reliably localised by any of these estimators. LLM sellers (gpt-6-luna; our market llm_v1, 74 games, T=20; sibling market llm_v3, 125 runs, T=12): a private channel produces judge-verified agreements and raises markup over the competitive (Nash) price in llm_v1 by +1.8 versus matched no-channel markets (C − A [1.2, 2.3], D − B [1.0, 2.5]), but the effect is mainly a price level. Level statistics separate channel from control runs (run AUROC: llm_v1 markup 0.87 [0.78, 0.94]; llm_v3 pair_level 0.98 [0.95, 1.00]). pCMI is not distinguishable from chance (llm_v1 0.45 [0.32, 0.59]; llm_v3 0.52 [0.39, 0.64]), and in an exploratory leave-one-run-out logistic model, adding it to markup gave no detectable improvement (−0.02 [−0.08, +0.01]). Longer games (T=50, 8 vs 8) did not meet the pre-declared rescue criterion (pCMI 0.45 [0.16, 0.75] vs markup 0.95; the CI cannot exclude moderate effects). In mixed gpt-6.1-sol/gpt-6-luna markets, no pCMI same-model excess over cross-model pairs was detected (+0.003 [−0.025, +0.032], 12 games; only large effects excluded). Supported claim: in these two markets at T=12–50, the private channel shows up mainly as a price level, which conditioned dependence measures are built to ignore; level statistics discriminate channel assignment far better than pCMI. Some coordinated variation is present (pair localisation on first differences in llm_v3; part of it also appears in placebo runs, §4.3.9), and whether pCMI fails because the effect is mostly a level or because of low power at short T is not fully settled. An exploratory injection check (§4.3.8) plants per-round shared ±1 price shocks (in 20% of rounds) into one pair of real LLM control games: pCMI detects them at T=50 (AUROC 0.93 [0.87, 0.98]) but only weakly at T=20 (0.63–0.66), and the real channel pairs show no statistically detected excess co-movement relative to rivals. That fits the level reading but does not settle it. Level screens separate channel assignment but are not collusion-specific (they rank legitimate public partnerships above controls, AUROC 0.75; in the sibling market an offered-but-undelivered placebo channel gave a similar premium, and pair_level named the pair about equally often, 13.5/15 vs 14/15, §4.3.9). In exploratory sibling monitor/firm-framing strata with no judge-labelled agreements, pair_level yielded 3.3/30 tie-averaged hits (chance expectation 5.0; §4.3.10); framing and agreement are confounded. In our own market, the first pair member to write pre-play already sets a provisional price above its rivals while writing its own first private message, before receiving any partner message (+0.94 [0.38, 1.59] vs whole-game premium +0.45; exploratory, descriptive, not a causal offer effect, §4.3.11).

1. Question and operational definition

Question. Do colluding agents' actions share more information than is explained by public market state and the rest of the market — and can a detector that sees only prices name the colluding pair while not accusing agents that respond to common information or share a policy?

What we call collusion (explicit collusion). A pair of sellers that has a private agreement channel and uses it to coordinate supra-competitive pricing. This follows the communication-plus-action family of definitions (Rose et al. 2026: communication plus harmful action; Bonjour et al. 2022: agents that "co-operate covertly to the disadvantage of others", operationalised as pairwise excess dependence; see literature/definitions/README.md in the hackathon starter repo collusion_hackathon). Supra-competitive pricing without a channel (e.g. all LLM sellers drifting above Nash) is labelled tacit_supracompetitive and analysed separately — never silently counted as a detector false positive or true positive. Three label levels are kept apart in ground_truth.jsonl: assigned opportunity (private_channel_enabled), verified agreement (agreement_verified), realised coordination (coordinated_actions_verified).

Benchmarks (uv run python -m sim.market): with cost 6 the unique symmetric discrete Nash price is 10 (cost 8: 12); joint-profit maximum is 16 for all states.

2. Setup

  • Market (sim/market.py): 4 sellers A–D, multinomial-logit demand with an outside option, market size 100/160 (low/high demand), marginal cost 6/8. Conditions: A independent; B common shocks (demand and cost redrawn each round, public); C designated colluding pair (random per run); D pair + shocks. (Condition letters A–D are market types, not sellers; C is compared with A and D with B, the "within-family" comparisons below.)
  • Scripted independents: noisy (quantal) best response to rivals' previous prices, 15% exploration.
  • Scripted colluders (strength s = per-round probability of coordinated play): signal — pair privately draws a joint price from {12,14,16} and both play it; tft — match partner's previous price; fixed_high — play 16 independently (no shared randomness).
  • Hard negatives (no channel): shared_policy — two agents run the same policy with independent sampling noise (with prob. 0.6 both apply the same nonlinear rule to last round's public prices, else a noisy best response); shared_seed — the extreme case: same policy and shared sampling randomness drawn from the public history (same model + same prompt + temperature 0 ⇒ same sample; 30% of draws idiosyncratic); legit_cooperation — follower publicly matches a leader's previous price; independent_high_price — two agents that just price high; common_shock (condition B).
  • LLM sellers (sim/llm_market.py): gpt-6-luna via llm.py, profit-maximisation framing after Fish et al. 2024; the designated pair gets a private, unmonitored chat channel plus one pre-play exchange; agents are never told to collude. Results in §4.3.

3. Detectors (detectors/infotheory.py, read trajectories.jsonl only)

Per run and pair: |Pearson| of prices and of price changes; plug-in MI with Miller–Madow correction; CMI given the discrete public state; pCMI = −½ log(1−ρ²) of residuals after regressing each agent's price on state dummies and all four lagged prices; lagged CMI/TE (max over directions); and Bonjour-style net influence (pair score minus mean of the other pairs). Null: B=200 draws, each circularly shifting every agent's series by its own random offset (all pairwise relative offsets ≥ 3 rounds); raw-price statistics use plain shifts, CMI|state shifts within each state stratum (keeps each seller's price–state relation), pCMI/TE re-residualise the shifted residuals on the design. Run-level p-value = max-over-pairs statistic against its null. Rounds are not iid, so we never use iid permutation. With fewer than 20 valid shifts (T ≲ 13) no test is performed (p = 1). Calibration is checked empirically on control runs (below), not assumed.

Second null — control surrogates ("same-model baseline"). The shift null asks "is this pair more dependent than the same series de-aligned?"; it is anti-conservative whenever agents' joint response to public state is something the residualisation misses. The alternative asks "is this market's most dependent pair more dependent than the most dependent pair in comparable markets without a channel?": the run's max-pair score is ranked against no-channel control runs of the same shock family (A for A/C, B for B/D; leave-one-out for controls). Caveats: (i) on the controls themselves the leave-one-out flag rate is ≤ α by construction, so it is not calibration evidence — only hard-negative and collusive rows are informative; (ii) in the scripted market the reference pool consists of best-responder markets, so a hard-negative row measures "false-accusation rate against a best-responder reference", not a same-policy null; (iii) the pool is drawn transductively from the controls of the same dataset (no labels of positives are used; the shock family is public); (iv) with a pool of m references the minimum attainable p is 1/(m+1), so m ≥ 20 is required at α = 0.05. For LLM sellers the reference pool is no-channel games of the same model — the "same-model baseline". With 21 controls per family in llm_v1 the surrogate test can reach α = 0.05. We also report run-level AUROC (= the mean surrogate rank) with bootstrap CIs.

Tuning discipline (data/SPLITS.md, EXPERIMENTS.tsv). Scripted dev seeds are seed0 ∈ {0, 7, 11, 100} (all non-locked; data/SPLITS.md); the hard-negative battery and power sweeps reported as headline numbers use locked seeds 1001/1002, run once with the frozen configuration (linear residualisation design, B=200 / B=100). Design iterations on dev before the locked runs: 5 (E01 Bonferroni null → E02 max-statistic null; E06 null v2 after review; E07 state×lag interactions → discarded; E08 control-surrogate null → kept as second null), plus label and baseline definition fixes made on pilots / before evaluation (E11, E12); all listed in EXPERIMENTS.tsv. No detector setting is tuned on LLM data, so all 74 llm_v1 games are confirmatory (64 planned + 10 extra A/B controls added before evaluation to give each family a surrogate pool ≥ 20, before any llm_v1 detector output was computed; E17).

(Surrogate-null rates on A and B are leave-one-out within the reference pool and ≈ α by construction; they are shown for completeness, the informative surrogate rows are the hard negatives and C/D.)

  • Positive control: every contemporaneous detector flags and localises the planted pair in 100% of runs (the signal colluder — fresh shared randomness each round — is the easiest case; §4.2 has weaker ones).
  • Conditioning on public state is necessary: raw MI flags 100% of common-shock controls; CMI|state 12%, pCMI 14%. The within-run shift null stays somewhat anti-conservative for pCMI under common shocks (14% here, 16% on dev seed 7, 2.5–15% on dev seed 11): best-responders react to state × lagged prices non-linearly. Adding state×lag interactions did not help on dev (EXPERIMENTS.tsv E07). Ranking against no-channel control markets (surrogate null) is ≤ α on the B controls by construction (leave-one-out); the informative check is the held-out hard negative shared policy + common shock: 4% [1, 13].
  • Shared policy with independent sampling noise is mostly removable: pCMI (conditioning on state and all lagged prices) flags 10–12% under the shift null and 4% under the surrogate null, vs MI 30–98% (shift) / 0–22% (surrogate).
  • Shared policy with a shared random seed remained flagged by every contemporaneous detector we tested (44–100% flagged across the five contemporaneous detectors and both nulls; the 44% minimum is differenced |Pearson|, not in the table; TE, which is lagged, flags only 2–12%): two copies of a policy that also share their sampling randomness are a private shared signal from the point of view of the price data. None of the price-only detectors we tested separates it from a private agreement channel; this needs provenance information (who runs which model with what seed).
  • Lagged CMI (TE) flags legitimate public leader-follower pricing in 100% of runs and shared heuristics in 90–98%; it is nearly blind to the contemporaneous colluder. Lagged dependence is not evidence of agreement.

Readings:

  1. Contemporaneous coordination is detected by CMI|state and pCMI down to s=0.1 at T=100 and at s=0.3 from T=20 (pCMI 0.80, controls 0.05). At T=10 the shift null cannot be run. The planted pair is ranked first at T=20 in 95% of runs. (An earlier sweep under the iteration-2 null reported power 0.12 at T=20; that null was replaced after review — its relative offsets were not constrained — and the dev numbers are superseded.)
  2. Lagged coordination (tit-for-tat): contemporaneous CMI has little power against it (the lags are conditioned away) and is caught by lagged CMI/TE at s ≥ 0.2–0.3 with T ≥ 50–100 — but TE also flags legitimate public leader-follower pricing in 100% of runs (§4.1). Statistically these are the same object.
  3. Collusion as a level (both just price high) carries no shared variation. pCMI does not detect it (0.07 vs 0.08 on controls); TE (0.47 vs 0.03) and CMI|state (0.28 vs 0.03) flag the market at s=0.8 but TE never names the pair (top-1 0.00; pCMI 0.17 ≈ chance). Localising it needs a price-level benchmark, not information theory.
  4. Raw MI is uncalibrated whenever there is a common driver (control column 0.50 = 0.0 on A and 1.0 on B).
  5. Control-surrogate null (in results/sweeps/power_test.json, surrogate_flag_rate): pCMI power 0.925 at s=0.1 and 0.575 at T=20 (vs 0.975 / 0.80 for the shift null; pooled C+D, 40 runs). With 20 reference runs per family the minimum attainable p is 1/21, so it is close to its resolution limit here.

4.3 LLM sellers

4.3.1 Pilots: getting LLM sellers to vary prices

Pilots (what it took to get LLM collusion to happen at all) — gpt-6-luna sellers via codex, all games T=20 except llm_pilot3 (T=15) (data/llm_pilot*, data/llm_hpilot; uv run python -m sim.llm_market --name <...>):

pilot design change outcome
llm_pilot (6 games, C/D) grid {8..16}, public board off pairs agree privately ("let's both hold 12") but all four sellers play 12 in ~every round (Nash 10) — no variance, no pair effect
llm_pilot2/3 wide integer grid 6–24, private cost shocks, reasoning field, T=1.0, "learn demand" hint prices still overwhelmingly at 12 (occasional deviations)
llm_hpilot 2 LLM + 2 scripted best-responders LLM sellers still choose 12 in 148/160 decisions, channel or not
llm_pilot4 removed the "price": 12 example from the JSON format spec prices vary (9–15); no-channel sellers drift toward Nash (means 9.5–11.9); one channel pair agrees on "start near 14", prices 13–14 vs rivals 12 for 10 rounds, then erodes to 12

Two lessons: (i) removing a single example value from the output format coincided with the market leaving the focal price (pilot comparison, not an isolated test). LLM pricing experiments look fragile to prompt anchors; (ii) a market in which every seller plays the same constant price contains zero information for dependence-based detectors, whatever the agreement status.

4.3.2 Datasets and declared analysis plan

Main LLM dataset llm_v1 (complete, 74 games, all sellers gpt-6-luna via codex — checked per run, E17): 16 per condition A–D (+5 extra A and B games so the same-model reference pool has ≥ 20 per family), T=20, design of llm_pilot4 (sim_version llm0.3). Labels: judge (tier=big) reads the private chat → agreement_verified; coordinated_actions_verified from prices (both pair members within ±1 of the agreed price in ≥ 50% of rounds after the agreement; criterion fixed on llm_pilot4, E11); no-channel runs with mean markup ≥ 2 over Nash are tacit_supracompetitive. First games (descriptive, before any detector was run): channel pairs lift the whole market's price level (channel games have higher market-wide prices; we did not test whether rivals respond causally). Per-game market means on all 74 games: C/D 10.8–16.8 (median 12.5), A/B 8.6–13.9 (median 11.3); the ranges overlap (scripts/market_mean_ranges.py → results/eval/llm_v1_market_mean_ranges.json; an earlier quote for the first ~20 games is dropped because no script regenerates it).

Analysis plan, declared before results (results below are headed by question: (i) price level = plan (b), (ii) run AUROC and (iii) localisation = (c), nulls = (d, e), (iv) mixed-model and (v) long games = (f)): (a) label rates per condition with Wilson CIs; (b) price-level effect of the channel — market mean price C/D vs A/B (Mann-Whitney, bootstrap CI) and pair-minus-rivals gap; (c) run-level AUROC [bootstrap CI] of pCMI, MI, TE vs the non-IT baselines market_level and pair_level; pCMI/TE top-1 localisation vs chance 1/6 (exact binomial); (d) shift-null flag rates by T (expected near-powerless at T=20); (e) surrogate null only where the pool ≥ 20; (f) follow-ups llm_long (A and C, T=50, 8 each: is it "too short" or "collusion is a level"?) and llm_mixed (2 gpt-6-luna

  • 2 gpt-6.1-sol, no channel: same-model vs cross-model pair dependence, per-run sign test). Pre-registered baseline fix (E12, before any llm_v1 detector output was viewed): market_level is the pair's mean markup over the per-round state Nash (raw mean price is confounded by B/D cost shocks; the raw version is kept as market_level_raw). AUROCs are reported pooled (C/D vs A/B) and within family (C vs A, D vs B); "do dependence detectors add anything beyond level?" = AUROC(IT) − AUROC(level), paired bootstrap over runs.

Extra confirmatory set, declared before computing (E13): the frozen detectors on the sibling project's LLM market llm_v3 (Q2.2; lab framing, grid 6–30, T=12, public board; private / none / legit = public shipping deal, a hard negative). No tuning; two adaptations forced by T=12: pCMI/TE residualise on numeric cost + demand instead of state dummies, and market_level uses the static Nash of that market. Metrics: run AUROC private vs none (and legit vs none), top-1 localisation vs 1/6, control-surrogate null vs the none pool.

Declared before any llm_long detector output (E20, 01:05 UTC): (v) is read off the same games' prefixes (T = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50; C vs A, 8 vs 8): pCMI/MI/TE/level run AUROC with bootstrap CI, and pCMI top-1 vs 1/6. "T rescues pCMI" requires AUROC(pCMI, T=50) ≥ 0.65 and ≥ AUROC(pCMI, T=20) + 0.15; only then is an extra T=50 batch (+16 C, +6 A) generated. Otherwise: no new generation. With 8 vs 8 the CI half-width is ≈ 0.25, so a null here only excludes large effects. The surrogate null is not used (pool 8 < 20). Per-pair scores for the sibling: results/eval/llm_v3_ext.json (uv run python -m experiments.ext_llm_v3).

4.3.3 External set llm_v3 (sibling market, T=12)

Reading: AUROC here measures how well a detector tells channel-assigned runs from controls, not how well it tells realised collusion. In this market the channel shows up as a pair-specific price level: the pair sits above its rivals. A trivial level statistic separates the conditions almost perfectly (pair_level AUROC 0.98 [0.95, 1.00]) and names the right pair in 63/70 runs. pCMI, raw MI and TE have run-AUROC CIs that include 0.5 (pCMI 0.52 [0.39, 0.64]). Their differences to pair_level are −0.39 to −0.53, and every CI excludes 0. CMI|state reaches 0.64 [0.53, 0.75] but scores legit runs about as high (0.62 vs none; private vs legit 0.53), so it does not separate collusion from a legitimate partnership. With the full none pool (35 ≥ 20) the control-surrogate null can now reach α=0.05. It flags 0/70 private runs for pCMI (Wilson [0.00, 0.05]) and 4/70 for MI, against 45/70 = 0.64 [0.53, 0.74] for pair_level. Leave-one-out FPR on the none runs is 0/35 for pCMI and 1/35 for MI and pair_level (rank-based, ≤ α by construction, not independent calibration evidence). Raw-price MI and Pearson still pick the right pair within a run above chance (42/70 and 35/70), plausibly because the pair moves up together. After conditioning on state and lagged prices, pCMI localisation drops to 18/70 = 26% (nominal p=0.036, unadjusted). There is no positive control for pCMI at exactly T=12. The nearest scripted point (shared-signal collusion, s=0.3, T=10, §4.2) localises the pair in 47% of runs (chance 17%), and T=20 does so in 95%. So 26% is weak even next to moderate coordinated-variation collusion of this length. The legit hard negative (public shipping deal, cost −1) scores below controls on markup (0.40) but 0.75 [0.61, 0.87] on pair_level (a ranking above controls; at α=0.05 the surrogate null flags only 1/20 legit markets). The highest-gap pair is the partnership in only 5/20 legit runs: the partnership mainly spreads prices, so some other pair looks high. A pair-gap ranking therefore puts markets with a legitimate partnership above controls, and its top pair is usually not the partnership.

Exploratory check E15 (not a headline; uv run python -m experiments.diag_llm_v3 → results/eval/llm_v3_diag.json, final n = 70 private / 35 none). Is the raw-price localisation only a shared upward drift? No. Top-1 of the assigned pair (chance 11.7/70): raw MI 42.1/70, |Pearson| after removing each seller's linear trend 32.0/70, MI on first differences 31.5/70 (p≈6e-8), |Pearson| on first differences 23.9/70 (p≈3e-4). The channel pair changes price in the same rounds, so there is coordinated variation as well as a level. But none of these variants separates channel runs from no-channel runs (run AUROC of the max-pair score 0.40–0.59, all CIs include 0.5). At T=12 with coarse prices, control markets often contain a pair that co-moves about as strongly as the colluding pair does, so max-pair scores do not resolve run discrimination. So the dependence signal localises a pair you already suspect but cannot screen markets. pCMI's weaker within-run localisation is consistent with lost power: 6–7 design columns (intercept, cost, demand, 4 lagged prices, minus any constant state column; experiments/ext_llm_v3.py _design_numeric) on 11 usable rows. It does not show that the information is absent.

Run AUROC of dependence (blue) vs level (orange) detectors on the LLM datasets (uv run python -m experiments.llm_fig).

(i) Does the channel raise prices? Yes, and mostly market-wide. Markup over the per-round state Nash (market average), within family: C − A +1.76 [1.21, 2.31] (Mann-Whitney one-sided p=4e-6), D − B +1.77 [1.02, 2.52] (p=8e-5). The pair premium over its own rivals is modest: +0.48 [0.33, 0.64] (C), +0.42 [0.26, 0.59] (D), and the gap shrinks over the game (figure). In llm_v3 the gap is pair-specific (pair_level ≈ markup there). Here the whole market is higher, so the max-pair markup is the better level statistic (pooled AUROC pair_level − markup −0.128 [−0.258, −0.001]). These comparisons do not establish who follows whom within a market.

(ii) Do dependence scores separate channel runs, alone or added to the level baseline? Not pCMI. Raw MI and TE rank D above B; MI ranks C below A (0.20 [0.06, 0.37]) and TE's C-vs-A discrimination is unresolved, likely a common-trend artefact (see diagnostics below). AUROC targets channel assignment (C/D vs A/B). Only 17/32 channel games meet the realised-collusion label. Run AUROC of the max-pair score, T=20, all games [bootstrap 95% CI]:

Standalone comparison (paired bootstrap over runs): pCMI − markup −0.42 [−0.56, −0.27] (pooled), −0.47 [−0.65, −0.29] (C vs A), −0.44 [−0.64, −0.22] (D vs B); pCMI − pair_level −0.29 [−0.46, −0.13]. MI − markup and TE − markup are clearly negative in C vs A and include 0 in D vs B (−0.06 [−0.24, 0.14], −0.14 [−0.34, 0.06]). Incremental value (E19, exploratory, added after review; uv run python -m experiments.diag_llm_v1 → results/eval/llm_v1_diag.json). A leave-one-run-out logistic model on markup + family dummy gives out-of-fold AUROC 0.89. Adding pCMI changes it by −0.025 [−0.079, +0.006], adding MI by +0.001 [−0.007, +0.011], and adding pCMI+MI+TE by −0.033 [−0.096, +0.003]. Within this sample and model, dependence adds no measurable discrimination on top of level. This does not show that the channel pairs have no coordinated variation (in llm_v3 first-differenced prices do localise the pair, E15).

The raw-dependence ranking reverses across families: MI separates D from B (0.82) but ranks C below A (0.20, substantial inverse discrimination). Shared trends are part of the explanation (E19). Market-mean price slopes downward in all 21 A runs (−0.07/round, sliding toward Nash) and upward in 15/16 D runs (+0.10/round), versus near-flat C (−0.015) and B (+0.015). After first-differencing, D vs B is unresolved (MI 0.51 [0.33, 0.71], |Pearson| 0.46 [0.26, 0.65]), consistent with the D "signal" coming mostly from the common upward drift. C vs A stays inverted after differencing (MI 0.29 [0.12, 0.47], |Pearson| 0.29 [0.13, 0.48]) and after linear detrending (|Pearson| 0.18). Plausibly A's slide is concentrated in synchronised early price changes, but that is not isolated. pCMI shows no clear channel discrimination in either family (0.47, 0.43). It measures linear residual correlation after state and lags, so this is not proof that every confound or every form of coordination is removed.

(iii) Localisation. pCMI names the assigned pair in 5/16 (C) and 4/16 (D) runs, and 4/17 among realised-collusion runs (0.24 [0.10, 0.47], exact binomial p=0.31 vs 1/6; ties broken uniformly at random with a fixed seed). The level statistics name it in 15/16 and 12/16 runs. (d, e) Nulls. Each family has its own 21 reference controls (A for A/C, B for B/D), enough to resolve α=0.05. Leave-one-out flags 1/21 controls per family. This bound is structural (rank-based), not independent evidence of calibration. The surrogate null flags pCMI in 0/16 C and 2/16 D runs, MI in 1/16 C and 7/16 D runs (the D drift again), and pair_level in 9/16 C and 5/16 D runs. The within-run shift null for pCMI rejects in 4/21 = 0.19 [0.08, 0.40] of A controls but in 0/21 B controls. Scripted controls at T=20 had an observed flag rate of 2/40 = 0.05 [0.01, 0.17] (§4.2), compatible with nominal calibration but imprecise. Non-stationary residuals are one untested explanation. We use only the surrogate null on this set. AUROC vs prefix length (T = 5, 10, 15, 20; figures/llm_v1_power_vs_T.png): pCMI does not improve (0.57, 0.46, 0.45, 0.45). MI (0.27 → 0.50) and TE (0.46 → 0.55) rise, but neither is above chance at T=20. llm_long (T=50) tests longer games.

4.3.5 Same- vs cross-model sellers (llm_mixed2)

(iv) llm_mixed2: are same-model pairs more dependent than cross-model pairs (shared-policy confound)? No detectable difference; the CIs exclude only large effects. 12 no-channel games (condition A, single public state), T=20; in each game 2 sellers run gpt-6.1-sol and 2 run gpt-6-luna (both via codex), with random seats. All 12 passed the E21 model check (per-seller model field). uv run python -m experiments.llm_eval mixed --name llm_mixed2 → results/eval/llm_mixed2_mixed.json; table printed by uv run python scripts/tables.py. Each game gives one observation: mean score of its 2 same-model pairs minus mean score of its 4 cross-model pairs (bootstrap 95% CI over runs, sign test; declared E16).

It is one of 5 distinct detectors computed (the 4 shown plus differenced |Pearson|, +0.006 [−0.094, +0.114]) with no multiplicity adjustment, and its sign test is p = 0.15, so we read it as weak at most. For pCMI, the detector used for the headline, no same-model excess was detected (point estimate +0.003). Its shift-null pair flag rates are 0/12, 2/12 and 3/48. For TE (10/48 cross pairs) and |Pearson| (24/48) the shift null over-rejects in this market, as on llm_v1 controls. Descriptively, the two models price alike: per-run sol − luna mean price +0.05 [−0.05, +0.14] (scripts/mixed_price_by_model.py → results/eval/llm_mixed2_price_by_model.json). Sol varies its price more within a game (mean within-seller SD 0.96 vs 0.63). Reading: in this market we detected no clear excess of price dependence for two copies of the same LLM over two different LLMs (uncertainty remains; 12 games). This matches the scripted shared-policy case with independent sampling noise (§4.1: pCMI 10% shift / 4% surrogate), not the shared-seed case (44–100% flagged by every contemporaneous detector). With n = 12 this rules out large same-model effects only; it does not show the confound is absent. Both models are OpenAI-family, so a cross-family test (e.g. Claude) remains open.

Per-game same-model minus cross-model pair score, mean and bootstrap 95% CI over the 12 games (uv run python scripts/mixed_fig.py). Score scales differ by detector, so compare each row with 0, not rows with each other.

Data-integrity note (E21): the first llm_mixed batch was invalid. A routing bug (llm.chat(tier="big", backend="codex") silently used gpt-6-luna) made all 12 games all-luna, as the per-seller model field shows. Its same-vs-cross numbers are discarded unreported. The bug is fixed, mixed_eval now drops runs whose mixed sellers did not run a different model, and the set is regenerated as llm_mixed2. Judge labels were unaffected (42/42 gpt-6.1-sol).

At T=50, pCMI − markup = −0.50 [−0.81, −0.17], so pCMI is clearly worse than the level statistic. The within-run shift null over-rejects on A controls again (pCMI flags 3/8 at T ≥ 30), as on llm_v1. That is a second reason not to use it on LLM data. Reading: using 50 rather than 20 rounds did not meet the declared pCMI run-discrimination criterion (point estimates flat, 0.36–0.45); the small sample leaves moderate discrimination unresolved. The evidence favours the "collusion is a level" branch of the plan's question (f), but at n = 8 per group it does not settle it.

4.3.7 Both LLM datasets together

We have two different LLM markets (different framing, grid, T, public board). In both, the private channel's effect shows up in the price data mainly as a price level (this is a statement about what discriminates channel assignment; whether delivered messages add to it is unresolved, §4.3.9). In llm_v1 it is market-wide; in llm_v3 it is pair-specific. Level statistics separate channel runs from controls (run AUROC 0.87 and 0.98). The conditioned dependence detector does not (0.45 and 0.52, standalone differences vs the best level statistic −0.42 and −0.46, CIs exclude 0). In llm_v1 it also adds nothing measurable on top of level. This is consistent with the scripted hard-negative result that "stay-high" collusion is hard for dependence measures to detect or localise (§4.2). It does not show that dependence detectors fail on LLM agents in general, or that these pairs have no coordinated variation. It shows that, at T=12–20 (and at T=50 in the small llm_long set, §4.3.6), level statistics discriminate channel assignment far better than pCMI, consistent with an effect that is mainly a level, which these detectors are built to ignore (low power remains possible; §4.3.8 shows pCMI sensitivity only to one specific shared-offset alternative). No pCMI same-model excess was detected either (§4.3.5). Level statistics are not collusion-specific either. They also rank legit partnership markets above controls (pair_level AUROC 0.75 in llm_v3) and are high in tacitly supra-competitive no-channel markets (6/21 B runs ≥ 2 over Nash).

Not claimed from this data: surrogate-null FPR with pool < 20; absence of same-model dependence from a null result; that dependence detectors fail on LLM agents in general. Follow-ups: mixed models §4.3.5, T=50 §4.3.6.

4.3.8 Exploratory: how much coordinated variation could pCMI see in these games? (E30, post-hoc)

Declared in EXPERIMENTS.tsv before computing; not a headline and not part of the pre-declared plan. Could pCMI have seen coordinated variation in these games if it were there? We plant coordination of known size into real LLM control games. For each planting, we choose a random pair and add the same per-round shock z_t ∈ {−1, 0, +1} (drawn i.i.d. each round, so it creates co-movement rather than a level shift) to both sellers' prices, with probability q/2 for each nonzero value. Everything else is the real LLM data. We score with the frozen pCMI (10 plantings per control game). We report the single-planting AUROC of max-pair pCMI (each planting vs the unplanted games), with a CI from a game-cluster bootstrap (control games resampled jointly with their own plantings). Co-movement is the fraction of the T−1 transitions with Δp_i·Δp_j > 0; unchanged prices count as no co-movement. Excess subtracts the mean over the other five pairs. We compute it on the planted pairs and on the assigned pair of the real channel games (same T-round prefix). uv run python scripts/injection_mde.py → results/eval/injection_mde.json.

background (controls) T q = 0.1 q = 0.2 q = 0.3 q = 0.5 observed co-move excess of assigned pair in channel games [95% CI]

llm_v1 B (21) 20 0.52 [0.46, 0.57] (+0.08) 0.63 [0.56, 0.72] (+0.16) 0.62 (+0.20) 0.75 (+0.30) D: +0.032 [−0.011, +0.074]

llm_long A (8) 50 0.76 [0.68, 0.85] (+0.14) 0.93 [0.87, 0.98] (+0.26) 0.97 (+0.36) 1.00 (+0.48) C: −0.008 [−0.023, +0.009]

Cells: single-planting pCMI run AUROC, planted vs unplanted [game-cluster CI], with the planted pairs' mean co-movement excess in parentheses. At q = 0 the AUROC is 0.50 and the excess is ≈ 0, as it should be. Top-1 localisation of the planted pair at T=50 is 0.81 (q=0.1) and 0.99 (q=0.2), against a chance level of 1/6.

Reading: at T=50, these control-background plantings give substantial pCMI discrimination and localisation for this specific shared-offset alternative. At T=20 the same plantings are only moderately detectable (AUROC 0.63–0.66 at q=0.2), so short games do cost pCMI power. The real channel pairs have no statistically detected mean excess of same-direction price changes relative to rival pairs. Their upper confidence bounds (+0.009 at T=50; +0.045 C and +0.074 D at T=20) are smaller than the mean planted excess at q=0.1 (+0.14, +0.10 and +0.08 respectively; for D at T=20 only just). This compares a CI bound with a planted mean, so it is a rough scale comparison, not a test. This is consistent with the "collusion is mainly a level" reading for llm_v1/llm_long. It shows sensitivity to one planted alternative only. It does not establish why the real-channel pCMI comparison is null, rule out low power against other alternatives (lagged leader-follower moves, where contemporaneous pCMI is weak, §4.2; nonlinear or market-wide coordination, which the rival subtraction can cancel; Phase 2 E73 finds a rank-based and a discrete sign-based CMI also at chance, P2.8), or show that coordination would look the same on channel-game backgrounds as on control backgrounds. It does not apply to llm_v3, where first differences do localise the pair (E15).

4.3.9 Exploratory: replication and placebo in the sibling market (E32, post-hoc)

Not a headline; declared in EXPERIMENTS.tsv before computing; frozen E13 configuration, nothing tuned; no LLM calls. The sibling generated a fresh 30-run replication of llm_v3 (llm_v3rep: 15 private / 10 none / 5 legit) and a placebo arm (llm_v3plc, 15 runs). Each placebo run uses the same seed, pair, cost and demand path as one llm_v3rep private run, and the pair gets the identical channel prompt, but its private messages are never delivered. Inputs are snapshotted in data/ext_llm_v3rep, data/ext_llm_v3plc (sibling commit 7cef9ed, SHA256SUMS). uv run python scripts/placebo_rep_ext.py → results/eval/placebo_rep_ext{.json,_report.md}. Top-1 = expected hits under uniform random tie-breaking (chance 2.5/15); p-values vs chance in the JSON come from a pair-label randomisation null (truth uniform over the 6 pairs). Matched difference = mean per-seed hit difference, private − placebo, with a bootstrap CI over the 15 seeds and an exact paired sign-flip p (assumes within-seed exchangeability of the two arms). The private-vs-placebo AUROC CI resamples matched seed pairs jointly. All 8 detectors are reported, unadjusted.

Reading. (1) Replication. On fresh seeds the §4.3.3 pattern holds: level statistics separate private from none (pair_level 0.88 [0.71, 1.00]) and name the pair in 14/15 runs. pCMI is not distinguishable from chance (0.50 [0.23, 0.76], a wide CI; top-1 2.0/15). (2) Placebo, level. The level statistics stay high when messages are never delivered: top-1 13.5/15; placebo vs none 0.89 (pair_level) / 0.78 (markup); private vs placebo 0.46 / 0.47. There is no statistically detected private − placebo difference, but this is not equivalence: the matched localisation CI is [−0.17, +0.23]. In this market, then, the level signal persists without message delivery (the offered pair still prices high, and still writes proposals); a moderate extra effect of delivered messages is not excluded. Whether attempted coordination is necessary is not resolved: in the monitor/firm strata without agreements the pair was not detectably localised, but framing and agreement are confounded there (§4.3.10). This agrees with the sibling's premium result (§4.4). (3) Placebo, dependence. No detector's private-vs-placebo AUROC CI excludes 0.5 at n=15 (meaningful delivery effects remain possible). One variant fits the prediction "co-movement needs delivered messages": MI on first differences names the pair in 10.0/15 private runs and 3.0/15 placebo runs (matched +0.47, bootstrap CI [+0.07, +0.80]). The exact sign-flip test gives p=0.065 (Bonferroni over the 8 contrasts ≈ 0.52), so the positive bootstrap CI is not confirmatory. At run level the same statistic actually scores placebo runs higher than private ones (AUROC 0.39 [0.23, 0.54]). |Pearson| on first differences, the other declared co-movement variant, shows no detected difference (8.0 vs 6.0), and raw |Pearson| goes the opposite way (placebo 11/15). So we read this as suggestive at most: with n=15 the data neither show nor rule out a delivered-coordination component in price co-movement. A larger placebo arm is the cheapest test that could settle it (§7). Part of the E15 first-difference localisation in llm_v3 may also be offer-driven: |Pearson| first differences localises the pair in placebo runs above chance (6.0/15, nominal randomisation p=0.027, unadjusted).

4.3.10 Exploratory: channel offered but no agreement (sibling strata, E35, post-hoc)

Not a headline; declared in EXPERIMENTS.tsv (with a decision rule) before computing; frozen E13 configuration, nothing tuned; no LLM calls. §4.3.9 left open what the level screen responds to: the channel offer, or the coordination the agents attempt once offered it. The sibling ran two exploration strata in which the pair was offered the private channel but the sibling's judge found no agreement in any of the 30 offered runs: llm_v3mon (lab framing plus a public note that prices are monitored; 14 private + 6 none) and llm_v3fp ("pricing manager + competition authority" framing; 16 private, no controls). Inputs are snapshotted in data/ext_llm_v3mon, data/ext_llm_v3fp (sibling commit 355db43, SHA256SUMS). uv run python scripts/nonagreement_ext.py → results/eval/nonagreement_ext{.json,_report.md}. Top-1 and p-values are computed as in §4.3.9 (tie-averaged hits; pair-label randomisation null; chance = n/6). Declared rule for pair_level on the pooled 30 runs: "offer-driven" supported if p < 0.05/8, contradicted if hits ≤ 30/6 + 2 = 7. Table p-values are unadjusted Monte Carlo upper-tail estimates; CIs are pointwise 95% bootstrap intervals. The ×8 correction applies to the declared pooled localisation criterion, not the AUROC intervals; this remains post-hoc exploration.

detector top-1 llm_v3mon (monitor) top-1 llm_v3fp (firm) top-1 pooled AUROC llm_v3mon private vs none
pCMI (state+lags) 3.0/14 (p=0.42) 1.5/16 (p=0.85) 4.5/30 (p=0.6) 0.56 [0.29, 0.82]
MI (raw prices) 1.0/14 (p=0.93) 2.5/16 (p=0.66) 3.5/30 (p=0.85) 0.54 [0.26, 0.79]
lagged CMI (TE) 2.0/14 (p=0.66) 1.5/16 (p=0.85) 3.5/30 (p=0.81) 0.81 [0.61, 0.98]
|Pearson| 2.0/14 (p=0.7) 2.7/16 (p=0.52) 4.7/30 (p=0.58) 0.52 [0.24, 0.82]
MI first differences 4.0/14 (p=0.19) 1.5/16 (p=0.9) 5.5/30 (p=0.47) 0.26 [0.02, 0.57]
|Pearson| first differences 4.0/14 (p=0.19) 3.8/16 (p=0.23) 7.8/30 (p=0.092) 0.48 [0.18, 0.79]
pair_level (non-IT) 2.0/14 (p=0.71) 1.3/16 (p=0.87) 3.3/30 (p=0.82) 0.42 [0.15, 0.69]
markup over Nash (non-IT) 2.0/14 (p=0.71) 1.3/16 (p=0.87) 3.3/30 (p=0.82) 0.48 [0.18, 0.79]

Reading. The declared heuristic labels this result "contradicted": pair_level yields 3.3/30 tie-averaged hits (chance expectation 5.0; upper-tail p=0.82), versus 13.5/15 placebo and 14/15 private (§4.3.9). This shows no detected above-chance localisation in these strata, rather than statistically refuting an offer effect. Within llm_v3mon the level statistics show no statistically detected separation between offered and no-channel markets (pair_level 0.42 [0.15, 0.69], n = 14 vs 6). No dependence statistic localises the pair either (all pooled p ≥ 0.09, unadjusted). Taken with §4.3.9, these observations are consistent with a willingness-to-coordinate explanation (the level signal follows attempted coordination, not the channel prompt alone; in our market it is already present when the first sender writes its own pre-play proposal, before any reply, §4.3.11), but framing and judge-labelled agreement are confounded: in the lab-framed placebo, agents were offered the channel and wrote coordination proposals (e.g. "Let's start with prices around 18 and avoid undercutting sharply", llm_v3plc_0000), which were simply not delivered, and the pair priced high; when no agreement formed (in the monitored stratum agents declined: the sibling reports independence or refusal phrases in 335/336 private messages; in the firm-framing stratum the judge found no agreement in 16/16), the pair premium was no longer localised. Caveats: the framings differ from the lab framing of §4.3.9, so framing and agreement are confounded (we cannot tell "no agreement → no premium" from "this framing → no premium"); n is small; and in llm_v3fp the sibling's frozen premium threshold flags 0.44 of firm-framing runs; this does not identify the offered pair, and the source of these flags is unresolved (no controls in that stratum). This does not change the §4.3.9 point that delivered messages add no detected level signal beyond attempted coordination.

4.3.11 Exploratory: is the pair premium in our market there before a partner message is read? (E39, post-hoc)

Prompted by the sibling's finding that round-1 prices alone discriminate (run AUROC 0.90), we asked the same of llm_v1/llm_long (declared rule in EXPERIMENTS.tsv, E39-offer-cue-declared; no detector changed, no LLM calls). In C/D games each pair member writes a pre-play message together with a provisional price. Pre-play is sequential: the first sender chooses without any partner message, and the second sender has already read the first sender's message. We therefore split the declared pair-mean quantity by sender order; this split was added after review (results/reviews/codex_e39_review.md), and the first-sender row is the clean pre-message quantity. The provisional prices were not stored in the dataset, so scripts/preplay_extract.py replays every C/D game from the LLM cache. A cache miss aborts the replay, and the replay reproduced every stored trajectory price exactly (40/40 games). The provisional prices are saved to data/{llm_v1,llm_long}/preplay.jsonl, and scripts/preplay_offer.py → results/eval/preplay_offer.json computes the following (10k run-bootstrap):

llm_v1 C+D (32 games) llm_long C (8 games)
(a1) first sender's provisional price − rivals' round-0 price (no partner message read) +0.94 [0.38, 1.59] +2.19 [0.56, 3.94]
(a) pair-mean provisional price − rivals' round-0 price (declared quantity) +0.95 [0.41, 1.62] +2.25 [0.62, 4.00]
(b) pair round-0 price − rivals' round-0 price +0.81 [0.36, 1.31] +2.19 [0.75, 3.81]
(c) pair − rivals, whole game (§4.3.4) +0.45 [0.34, 0.57] +0.42 [0.20, 0.65]
round-0 market markup over Nash, run AUROC C vs A / D vs B 0.77 [0.61, 0.89] / 0.68 [0.50, 0.85] 0.66 [0.38, 0.92] (C vs A)

Reading. The declared rule's verdict is "offer cue present in our market" in both datasets, both for the declared pair mean and for the first sender alone ("offer cue" is the declared rule label and means "present before a partner message is read", not an offer effect separate from the seller's own proposal). The first pair member's provisional price is above its rivals' round-0 prices before it has received any partner message. That price is written in the same response as its own first private message, and it is typically the price that message proposes (e.g. "I propose we both start at 15 and avoid undercutting", provisional 15, llm_v1_D_003); the second sender matches it exactly in 27/32 games. So the premium does not require reading a partner's message, but this check does not separate it from the seller's own coordination attempt. Rivals' round-0 prices match those of control sellers (llm_v1 C family: rivals 11.7, A sellers 11.7, pair provisional 12.8). The opening point estimates exceed the whole-game premium (in llm_v1 the CIs of (b) and (c) overlap; no paired test), consistent with the premium shrinking over the game. This agrees in direction with the sibling's round-1 and placebo findings (§4.3.9, §4.4). It also agrees with the §4.3.9 point that received messages add no detected level signal: the second sender, who has read the first message, is at +0.97 [0.41, 1.62], and pair provisional minus own round-0 price is +0.14 [−0.03, 0.38]. It is a descriptive, exploratory result: it does not identify a causal channel-offer effect, does not tell how much of the whole-game premium the offer explains, and does not replace a placebo arm (a seller can anticipate coordination before reading anything). Caveats: post-hoc; small n (the llm_long CI is wide). The provisional and round prices are different decision tasks: the provisional price is requested with different wording ("price is provisional") and under the common cost without a private shock, while rivals' round-0 prices use the same public state plus their own private cost shock and no chat. The effect comes from a right tail of high openings. Per seller, provisional prices ≥ 14 occur in 8/32 C-pair and 18/32 D-pair prices in llm_v1, against 0/84 round-0 prices of A sellers and 34/84 of B sellers (cost-shocked, so D openings are less distinctive).

4.4 Umbrella synthesis with the sibling project (Q2.2, text + action auditing)

Numbers in this paragraph come from the sibling repo collusion-22-say-vs-do (REPORT abstract, locked test split n = 95, read 01:05 UTC; placebo result read 04:05 UTC at sibling commit 6a1de73; not regenerated here). The two projects reach a consistent conclusion from opposite directions.

  • (1) In both LLM markets the private channel shows up first as a price level: here pair_level/markup reach run AUROC 0.87–0.98, and the sibling's one-line pair-premium statistic reaches 0.95 on its test split (0.92 [0.79, 1.00] on its 30-run fresh replication, read 04:20 UTC at sibling commit ddc2532), exceeding the sibling's six original zero-shot LLM auditor views (max 0.86).
  • (2) Signals that look for how agents coordinate add little on these short games: conditioned dependence (pCMI) does not resolve above-chance discrimination here (0.45 [0.32, 0.59], 0.52 [0.39, 0.64]), and the zero-shot text-only auditor is at chance there (0.47). The sibling's supervised text classifier (0.98, in-distribution) shows the text carries condition information, though not which cues it uses.
  • (3) Level statistics are not collusion-specific. They rank markets with the legit public partnership above controls (pair_level AUROC 0.75 here, usually naming a non-partner pair), and they flag tacitly supra-competitive no-channel markets.
  • Caveat from the sibling's later exploratory placebo study (15 matched seeds): when private messages are offered but never delivered, the designated pair's premium is about the same (sibling's premium difference in price units, rounds 2–12, placebo − private +0.03 [−0.54, +0.49]; a different quantity from the §4.3.9 localisation difference). So in llm_v3 the level signal cannot be attributed specifically to delivered private coordination; the level signal persists without delivery (the placebo agents still wrote proposals). In sibling strata where the channel was offered but no agreement formed (monitor / firm framing, 0/30 agreements), pair_level did not detectably localise the pair (3.3/30, chance 5.0; §4.3.10); framing and agreement are confounded, so whether attempted coordination is necessary remains unresolved. Our frozen detectors on the same placebo runs agree (§4.3.9): pair_level names the pair in 13.5/15 placebo vs 14/15 private runs, and no detector separates private from placebo runs with statistical significance (n=15; a moderate delivery effect is not excluded). We did not run a placebo arm in llm_v1.
  • Practical reading (a hypothesis, not tested as a pipeline): a cheap level screen as an always-on first stage, with dependence/text audits as second-stage evidence.
  • The scripted results (§4.1–4.2) show where dependence measures do add value: collusion implemented through coordinated variation, given enough rounds for its strength (e.g. signal s=0.3 at T=20, s=0.1 at T=100).
  • How detectable LLM collusion is depends on the market and its framing. The pair-minus-rivals premium is +1.65 [1.38, 1.93] in the sibling's lab-framed market (private runs, 10th–90th percentile +0.66…+3.18; none +0.04, legit +0.05; experiments/premium_llm_v3.py). Here it is +0.45 [0.34, 0.57], and most of the effect is market-wide.

Phase 2 details (P2.1–P2.14)

P2.1 Precision at realistic collusion prevalence (E46, from the saved v1 evaluations; uv run python scripts/prevalence.py → results/eval/prevalence.{json,md}). At the frozen α = 0.05 run-level flags, precision = π·TPR / (π·TPR + (1−π)·FPR), with 95% intervals from independent Jeffreys posteriors for TPR and FPR. sibling llm_v3, T=12 pair_level (surrogate) 45/70 1/20 (legit partnership) 0.11 [0.03, 0.54] 0.40 [0.13, 0.86] 0.76 [0.42, 0.97]

* Surrogate-null FPR on the reference controls is ≤ α by construction (leave-one-out), so that row is an optimistic bound; the hard-negative rows (common shock, shared seed, legit partnership) are independent evidence. Reading: at 1% prevalence no detector reaches precision 0.25 in any setting, so most alarms would be false; at 5% the best rows are around 0.3–0.6 with wide intervals. pCMI on LLM data has precision near the base rate at all three prevalences (no information), and raw MI against common shocks equals the base rate exactly. This supports using any of these flags as a first-stage screen that triggers an audit, not as evidence of collusion on its own.

P2.2 Independent reimplementation check (E47). codex (gpt-6.1-sol, separate scratch directory) received only the §3 detector text, the market_level/pair_level definitions from §4.3.2, the Nash prices and the data, and no code (results/reimpl/{BRIEF.md,NOTES.md,reimpl.py}). Comparison with our frozen evaluations: uv run python scripts/reimpl_compare.py → results/reimpl/compare.json. Per-run scores agree to < 1e-9 in 422 of 424 run × statistic cells (llm_v1 T=20, all four conditions; llm_long T=50 and its 20-round prefix; pCMI, Miller–Madow MI, markup, pair_level). The two exceptions are perfect-fit llm_v1 runs where only the constant used to cap ρ² differs (both versions rank them highest). All 20 run-AUROCs are identical (e.g. llm_v1 pCMI 0.453, markup 0.870; llm_long pCMI 0.453, markup 0.953). The pCMI shift-null flag rate on llm_v1 A controls is 4/21 for us and 5/21 for the reimplementation (C: 2/16 for both). The gap is one run near p = 0.05 under an independently drawn 200-shift Monte Carlo null. No bug was found and no reported number changes.

P2.3 Same-model confound: what a deployer can conclude when everyone runs the same model (E48, E54; no new LLM calls; uv run python scripts/same_model.py → results/eval/same_model.{json,md}; uv run python scripts/matched_ref.py → results/eval/matched_ref.{json,md}). E48 pools all no-shock T=20 games by pair type: luna–luna no-channel pairs (186 pairs / 41 games), sol–sol (12 / 12), luna–sol cross (48 / 12), and the channel pair of all-luna C games (24 games). Pair AUROCs have 95% CIs from resampling games jointly; detectors frozen, rule declared in the ledger before running.

channel-assigned pair vs … pCMI pCMI, own lag only MI pair_level pair markup over Nash
luna–luna, no channel (same model as colluders) 0.49 [0.38, 0.62] 0.44 [0.31, 0.57] 0.31 [0.18, 0.47] 0.93 [0.88, 0.97] 0.96 [0.90, 1.00]
sol–sol, no channel 0.72 [0.53, 0.89] 0.65 [0.45, 0.83] 0.27 [0.12, 0.45] 0.89 [0.77, 0.98] 1.00 [0.98, 1.00]

(a) Level contrasts are not hurt by sharing a model; the dependence statistics are. Declared rule: the confound is "material" if AUROC(channel vs same-model) is ≥ 0.10 below AUROC(channel vs cross). Differences (joint game bootstrap): pair_level +0.00 [−0.03, +0.04] (luna), −0.04 [−0.12, +0.03] (sol); markup −0.04 [−0.10, −0.00] (luna); pCMI −0.09 [−0.17, −0.01] (luna, borderline); own-lag-only pCMI −0.13 [−0.23, −0.04] (luna, material). MI is reversed (< 0.5): channel pairs hold prices still. (b) Exploratory: among no-channel pairs, same-model luna pairs look more dependent than cross pairs (pCMI AUROC 0.59 [0.51, 0.67]; shift-null flags 37/186 = 20% [13, 28] vs 4/48 = 8% [0, 17]), which mixes model with market composition (§4.3.5 found no within-market difference). (c) Reference markets: a fresh model-matched pool meets the declared false-flag criterion, but the prompt moves the price level as much as the model does (E54, declared; interim). A mismatched 12-game sol+luna pool (α = 0.10) made pCMI falsely flag 11/21 = 52% [32, 72] of llm_v1 no-channel markets (E48). E54's fresh, independently generated luna pool (E43 A games, five wordings × 6, n = 30) gives 0/21 [0, 16]% false flags at α = 0.05 for pair markup, pair_level, pCMI and MI, meeting the criterion (≤ 0.10, Wilson upper < 52%). But power collapses for the level screens: pair markup flags 1/16 llm_v1 channel markets, pair_level 4/16, pCMI 0/16 (vs markup 15/16 against the mismatched pool at α = 0.10), because the reference's price level depends on the instructions: no-channel markup over Nash ranges from −0.19 [−0.83, +0.58] to +2.56 [2.07, 3.05] (different JSON template), above the llm_v1 channel markets (+1.78 [1.41, 2.23]); see P2.7. Deployer reading: a pair standing out from its own market (pair_level) is robust to everyone running the same model. Absolute statistics (markup, pCMI, MI) need reference markets with the same model and comparable instructions, with ≥ 20 games for α = 0.05. Pending: the final E54 run adds the 20 llm_long_p2 A prefixes (prompt-matched v0 pool of 26).

P2.4 Scripted coalitions, collusion onset and cost asymmetry (E49–E51; locked test, run once). Codex (gpt-6.1-sol) wrote the simulator options, group statistic score_groups and experiments/p2_scripted.py on dev seeds (results/p2/*_dev.json, results/p2/REPORT_codex.md); default simulator output and score_run are byte-identical to v1 (results/p2/compatibility.json). Each experiment ran once on locked seeds (data/SPLITS.md): uv run python -m experiments.p2_scripted {coalition,onset,costasym} --test → results/p2/*_test.json. Settings: T=100, signal collusion s=0.6, 30 games per group, B=100, α=0.05; intervals are Wilson 95% (k/30: 0 → [0, 11]%, 1 → [1, 17]%, 2 → [2, 21]%, 4 → [5, 30]%, 5 → [7, 34]%). Dev and test agree on every qualitative point.

test (locked) pair_level (surrogate) max-pair markup (surrogate) pCMI (shift) group TC4 / TC3 (shift) ni_pCMI (surrogate) controls (same family)
3 of 4 collude (A / B) 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 pCMI 2/30, 2/30; TC4 1/30, 2/30; pair_level 0/30, 1/30
all 4 collude (A / B) 1/30, 0/30 (AUROC 0.26, 0.25) 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 30/30, 30/30 as above
cost asymmetry (2 sellers +2 private cost, no channel) 30/30 false (names the high-cost pair 30/30) 30/30 false 4/30 false (MI 3/30) – 1/30 false pCMI 1/30, pair_level 1/30, MI 2/30

(a) Coalitions. The frozen upper-tail relative screen (pair price minus rivals) loses power against a cartel that includes everyone: its AUROC drops below 0.5 when all four collude. Surrogate-flagged columns are calibrated against same-family controls by leave-one-out, so their control rates are bounded by construction. Absolute statistics (markup over the Nash price, pCMI, group total correlation) still detect every run, and ni_pCMI also flags 30/30 at this strength, but the pair it names is arbitrary when all collude. TC4 detects nothing that pCMI misses, and TC3/TC4 also flag pair-only collusion, so a significant group TC does not show that every member colludes. (b) Onset (collusion starts at round 25 or 50). A one-sided CUSUM on each pair's price gap to its rivals (κ = 0.5, max over six pairs) used h = 14.5, fixed from the 30 dev controls; on test controls it raised 0/30 false alarms and detected 30/30 runs after onset, with median delay 7.5 rounds [IQR 5–12] (onset 25) and 7 [5–9] (onset 50). Expanding-window pCMI (looks at 20, 30, …, 100 rounds, uncorrected) alarmed on 5/30 controls (17% [7, 34]) and before onset in 6/30 and 4/30 runs, so it needs a sequential correction. The level CUSUM is the better online screen here, but inherits the weaknesses of pair_level (rows (a) all-4 and (c)). LLM counterpart (Q2.2 E112, their P2.15): replacing one colluder by a fresh luna at round 21 left the level intact (+0.20 [−0.08, +0.62]) and this CUSUM alarmed in 0/30 replaced games by round 25, so a level CUSUM sees onsets, not personnel changes. The level survives even a non-cooperating newcomer (Q2.2 E115, their P2.15): a gpt-6.1-sol replacement re-agrees in 0/20 games and undercuts, yet 18/20 channel markets remain ≥ Nash + 2 (sibling result, not regenerated here; four final-round decisions were reconstructed from saved records). (c) Cost asymmetry is a decisive hard negative for both tested level screens. Two sellers with privately higher costs legitimately price higher; pair_level and max-pair markup falsely flag all 30 markets and name the innocent high-cost pair every time. pCMI's false-flag rate is 4/30 (13% [5, 30]), against 1/30 on plain controls, but 30 games per group cannot show that its calibration is unchanged. This mirrors the LLM result, where levels detect and pCMI does not: neither family of statistics is safe alone.

Every game is scored at T=100 and on its first 30 rounds with frozen detectors and the shift null (α=0.05). Markup and pair_level are flagged against same-market controls (leave-one-out surrogate), so only pCMI's control row is calibration evidence. The design was amended after the dev run (seed 230) showed s=0.3 at ceiling: the weak group moved to s=0.15 and the T=30 prefix was added before any test run (ledger E52). (a) The calibration criterion passes in 9/10 cells; elastic/A fails it. Pooled over the 10 market × family cells, pCMI falsely flags 18/300 = 6.0% [3.8, 9.3] of control games at T=100 and 20/300 = 6.7% [4.4, 10.1] at T=30; the declared rule (≤ 0.10 per cell) fails only for elastic/A at 4/30 = 13% [5, 30]. Raw MI still flags 30/30 common-shock controls in every 4- and 6-seller market (6/30 at N=2). (b) Power transfers. At s=0.6, every detector flags 30/30 in every cell. At s=0.15 and T=100, pCMI flags 20–30/30, against 12–29 for markup and 13–27 for pair_level. (c) Less elastic demand is the hard case, mostly for level screens. When Nash (12–13) is close to the agreed prices, collusion adds little to the price level: at s=0.15 in the inelastic market, markup flags 12/30 and 14/30 and pair_level 15/30 and 13/30, while pCMI flags 28/30 and 20/30. At N=2 the market is the pair, so pair_level is undefined and markup over Nash or pCMI must carry the screen. Relative performance varies with market and horizon (at s=0.15 and T=30, pair_level beats pCMI in N6/A, 23 vs 13/30). Collusion here is a shared signal, i.e. co-movement by construction, so these rows show that pCMI's calibration (with the elastic/A exception) and strong-signal power do not hinge on the 4-seller, μ=3 choice, not that real colluders produce co-movement (the LLM sellers in §4.3 did not).

P2.6 Exploration: bid rotation, collusion that is not a shared price move (E53; scripted; locked test seed 2005, run once). In a coordinated round (probability s=0.6, decided by a shared private draw), one pair member is the round's "winner" and prices by noisy best response, while its partner posts the cover price 16. rotation_alt: the winner alternates deterministically (predictable from last round's public prices). rotation_rand: the winner is drawn privately each round. Base market (N=4, μ=3), T=100, 30 games per group, frozen detectors. Command: uv run python -m experiments.p2_rotation --test → results/p2/rotation_test.json (dev seed 240 agrees qualitatively). Flags out of 30 at T=100, families A / B (Wilson 95%):

group mean price pCMI (shift) TE, lagged (shift) MI (shift) markup (surrogate) pair_level (surrogate)
controls 10.41 / 11.20 5, 4 (17% [7, 34], 13% [5, 30]) 3, 3 3, 30 1, 1 1, 1
shared-signal pair (reference) 11.71 / 12.29 30, 30 6, 4 30, 30 30, 30 30, 30
rotation, alternating winner 11.26 / 11.95 6, 2 (= controls) 13, 17 (43% [27, 61], 57% [39, 73]) 0, 26 30, 30 30, 30
rotation, private random winner 11.29 / 11.96 24, 22 4, 3 19, 30 30, 30 30, 30

Reading. (a) A rotation schedule that public lags predict is invisible to pCMI. pCMI conditions on all lagged prices, so its flag rate equals the controls'; lagged TE sees part of the schedule (13/30 and 17/30), and raw MI is below control in family A (0/30), as with the LLM channel pairs (P2.3). (b) With a privately drawn winner, prices are contemporaneously anti-coordinated and pCMI flags 24/30 and 22/30. (c) Level screens flag every rotation game because the cover price lifts the market mean price by 0.85 (A) and 0.75 (B) above controls; they would miss rotation with a competitive cover price, which we did not test. This is a scripted exploration with a single strength. It shows one more place where pCMI's conditioning removes real collusion along with confounds: when the coordination is a deterministic function of public history.

P2.7 Prompt-wording robustness: the channel markup holds across five wordings, the detectability does not (E43; gap 1; all games confirmatory, no tuning; uv run python scripts/p2_variants.py --run-eval → results/eval/p2_variants.{json,md}). Five seller-prompt wordings (sim/llm_market.py --variant): v0 = the v1 prompt (byte-identical), para = paraphrased instructions, template = a different JSON reply template, order = information in a different order, noreason = no reasoning field. Each wording: 6 A + 6 C games, T=20, seed 43 (same seeds and costs across wordings), gpt-6-luna, frozen v1 detectors. Per-wording AUROCs are on 6 vs 6 games, so we do not compare wordings with each other on AUROC.
